sections.title: INTRODUCTION

summary.text: Introduces WHO's series of PrEP implementation modules, developed after the 2015 recommendation that oral PrEP be offered to people at substantial risk of HIV. It notes that PrEP should not displace established prevention methods, that key populations may face legal and social barriers, and that individuals decide whether to use it. It describes the audience, guiding principles and the content of each module.

sections.extract: Following the WHO recommendation in September 2015 that “oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) should be offered as an additional prevention choice for people at substantial risk of HIV infection as part of combination HIV prevention approaches”, partners in countries expressed the need for practical advice on how to consider the introduction of PrEP and start implementation. In response, WHO has developed this

sections.title: THE COUNSELLORS MODULE

summary.text: Defines the counsellors module as intended for lay, peer and professional counsellors and health workers who counsel PrEP users, distinguishing it from community education. It restates WHO's PrEP recommendation and that PrEP should not undermine condom programming or harm reduction.

sections.extract: This module is for staff in clinical and other settings who counsel PrEP users. Those who counsel PrEP users may be lay, peer or professional counsellors and healthcare workers including nurses, clinical officers and doctors. This module does not include information about community education; that is the focus of the module for community educators and advocates. Community education can shape awareness of and demand

sections.title: Counselling goals related to PrEP

summary.text: Outlines the goals of PrEP counselling at initiation and follow-up, including exploring sexual health and drug use, building prevention and fertility plans, and addressing adherence and disclosure challenges.

sections.extract: The goals of counselling depend on whether the client is starting PrEP or is already using PrEP. Counselling may explore current sexual health and drug use protection plans and raise awareness about PrEP and other prevention strategies. Mixing sexual health education with client-centred discussion (see below) can facilitate open communication about sexual health desires, goals and plans. Counsellors can help clients

sections.title: PrEP and “seasons of risk”

summary.text: Explains that HIV exposure is often episodic, so PrEP users move through 'seasons of risk' and need to learn when to start and stop PrEP. It encourages counsellors to discuss with users how long they plan to use PrEP and how they will decide it is no longer needed.

sections.extract: People often move in and out of “seasons of risk” and “risky situations” for HIV infection. For both antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV treatment and PrEP, adherence is crucial. However, adherence to ART involves lifelong therapy with daily doses. In contrast, among PrEP users, HIV exposure may be episodic. sections.title: Who can counsel about PrEP?

summary.text: Discusses who can counsel on PrEP, stressing training, refresher training and respect for user preferences between peer, lay or medically trained counsellors. It supports a role for lay and peer counsellors under supportive supervision by trained professionals.

sections.extract: Counsellors and health workers should be carefully trained on PrEP use before they counsel clients about PrEP. In addition, the user’s preferences should be considered. Some users may prefer talking with a peer or lay counsellor, who has some shared experiences. Others may prefer counselling from a medically trained counsellor (for example, a nurse, doctor or clinical officer). Integrating training on PrEP

sections.title: Counselling strategies

summary.text: Sets out PrEP counselling strategies, beginning with culturally relevant group activities and support groups, with examples from trials in the United States and sub-Saharan Africa. It describes principles for individual counselling, such as cultural sensitivity, client-centredness, autonomy and attention to unmet needs, and lists related services like mental health and violence counselling. It covers concerns for specific groups including serodiscordant couples and transgender people. It ends with sample follow-up questions on social experiences, sexual behaviour, HIV test results and plans for staying HIV- and STI-negative.

sections.extract: Specific information about PrEP in client-friendly language is available in the module for PrEP users. sections.title: Differentiated care

summary.text: Suggests that PrEP programmes explore differentiated care, as in HIV and TB services, giving more intensive support to those who need it. It mentions ART approaches such as adherence clubs, streamlined visits and longer intervals between visits for users doing well.

sections.extract: As with HIV and TB care, PrEP programmes could consider the potentially facilitating role of differentiated care. To date there is little experience of differentiated care approaches in PrEP services, but this is something that could be explored as services evolve and mature. sections.title: Monitoring efforts

summary.text: Urges programmes to consult communities on PrEP users' needs and to monitor adherence, retention and stopping and restarting PrEP as part of quality improvement.

sections.extract: As noted, developing strategies and programmes that are tailored to the needs of the specific community or PrEP user population presents the best opportunity for high quality, client-centred care. sections.title: Counselling example I: Integrated Next Step Counselling (iNSC)

summary.text: Describes Integrated Next Step Counselling, a brief, client-centred, problem-solving method developed for the iPrEx study to support PrEP choice, adherence and sexual health planning. It outlines its steps and explains that it is linked to delivering negative HIV results, combining test counselling and adherence counselling in one conversation.

sections.extract: This method was developed to address the challenges of informing the choice of PrEP, developing a plan for adherence, and developing broader plans for sexual health (17). The method is interactive, brief, client-centred and focused on problem-solving, starting with the client’s identification of personal goals and the barriers and facilitators to achieving those goals. The method was developed for the iPrEx study

sections.title: Counselling example II: Informed choice counselling

summary.text: Presents an informed choice counselling approach developed by FHI360 for women at higher HIV risk in Kenya and South Africa, built on principles of voluntary, informed decision-making. It walks through four phases (introductory, informational, deliberation and decision, and confirmation) with suggested counsellor prompts. A flow chart shows how to assess interest in PrEP and develop either a PrEP use plan or a risk-reduction plan.

sections.extract: Best practices in counselling are also incorporated into a PrEP counselling plan that was developed by FHI360 for a study looking at PrEP use and risk compensation among women at higher risk for HIV infection at sites in Kenya and South Africa (24, 25).
